I am a 50-year-old woman farmer in Quzhou County, and I have been farming this land since I was a young girl. I never went to school, but I know my fields well. In our village, everyone grows winter wheat and summer maize in rotation — that is the way of the North China Plain, and it is what feeds my family and puts a little cash in my pocket. I have about 5 mu of good flat land, and I am not going to take chances with strange crops like stevia or chili. My husband and I are getting older, and our children work in the city, so we need a system we can manage without too much risk.

This year, I will plant winter wheat in the autumn after the corn comes out, just like always. I will buy improved wheat seed — probably something like Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22 — from the village supply store, because the old traditional seeds do not yield enough anymore. Before sowing around October 1st, I will rotary-till the soil to break up the stubble and prepare a good seedbed. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dose at sowing, and then top-dress with urea in the spring when the wheat starts to green up. I usually irrigate three or four times: once for winter irrigation, once at green-up, once at jointing, and maybe once at heading if the spring is dry. For pests, I will spray herbicide once to control weeds, and insecticide twice — once in spring and once if I see aphids or armyworms. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the weather is decent.

After I harvest the wheat around early June, I will immediately plant summer maize — Denghai 605 or another hybrid — using no-tillage direct seeding. There is no time to plough; the season is short and we must catch the rains. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat; I will water it twice, once at sowing and once at the big trumpet stage if it does not rain. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and maybe a side-dressing of urea when the plants are knee-high. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide twice, because corn borers and armyworms are a real problem in our area. If all goes well, I should get about 550 kg per mu of maize.

This is my plan. It is not fancy, but it has kept food on the table for decades.
